patches.old: which is why cell-wall synthesis inhibitors like penicillin are ineffective against *Chlamydia*.
patches.new: which is part of why cell-wall synthesis inhibitors like penicillin are not used against *Chlamydia* (see the note on chlamydial peptidoglycan below for the rest of the reason).

patches.old: Consider endotoxin release... but wait — *S. aureus* is gram-*positive* and lacks LPS.
patches.new: Endotoxin release is the reflex answer, but it cannot be right here: *S. aureus* is gram-**positive** and has no LPS at all.

patches.old: *Chlamydia* is an obligate intracellular pathogen; it also lacks a classic peptidoglycan layer. Penicillin cannot reach the intracellular compartment and has no target even if it could.
patches.new: *Chlamydia* is an obligate intracellular pathogen, and penicillin penetrates host cells poorly. Older textbooks add that *Chlamydia* has no peptidoglycan at all; that claim is now out of date and is worth getting right, because it was a famous puzzle. *Chlamydia* carries the genes for peptidoglycan synthesis and is sensitive to drugs that target it, yet for fifty years nobody could detect any peptidoglycan in it — the so-called **chlamydial anomaly**. Newer labelling methods resolved it: pathogenic *Chlamydia* do make peptidoglycan, but instead of the full sacculus that surrounds an ordinary bacterium, they build only a narrow ring at the division septum, used for cell division and otherwise absent. So the accurate statement is that *Chlamydia* lacks a conventional peptidoglycan cell wall, not that it lacks peptidoglycan. Either way the clinical conclusion is the same — beta-lactams are not the treatment.

sources.title: Liechti et al., “A new metabolic cell-wall labelling method reveals peptidoglycan in Chlamydia trachomatis”, Nature (2013) — peptidoglycan detected, localized mainly to the septum of dividing cells

visual.title: Five targets, and the four replies
visual.alt: A schematic bacterial cell marking the five druggable targets — the peptidoglycan wall, the cell membrane, the 70S ribosomes, DNA gyrase and folate synthesis — each annotated with why the human equivalent differs or is absent; a panel listing the drug classes at each target with the single fact each is tested on; and a panel presenting the four resistance mechanisms as replies: destroy the drug, change the lock, pump it out, and shut the door.
visual.caption: Each target is something you do not have — that absence is the entire safety margin, which is why there are so few of them.
